--- Page 1 ---
Routing and Cache Retention for Multi-Turn LLM
Inference: Theory and Implementation
Sentao Miao∗
Leeds School of Business, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO 80309, USA, sentao.miao@colorado.edu
Tianjiao Nie∗
Qiuzhen College, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China, nietj21@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn
Yuan Zhou∗†
Yau Mathematical Sciences Center & Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China;
Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Beijing 101408, China, yuan-zhou@tsinghua.edu.cn
Song Yuan
StepFun Intelligence, Shanghai 200232, China, oliveryuan@stepfun.com
Yuanwei Lu
StepFun Intelligence, Shanghai 200232, China, luyuanwei@stepfun.com
Yibo Zhu
StepFun Intelligence, Shanghai 200232, China, zhuyibo@stepfun.com
Multi-turn AI agents execute iterative loops of large language model (LLM) inference and external tool calls,
transforming cluster serving into a dynamic resource-allocation problem where routing and key–value (KV)
cache retention jointly govern prefix reuse across inter-turn delays. We formulate a fluid approximation of
this system and show that optimal admission, routing, and eviction are governed by endpoint-specific shadow
prices for computation and memory together with session continuation values. Building on this structure,
we propose an asymptotically optimal buffer-reserve policy that absorbs stochastic fluctuations using a
vanishing share of capacity. To handle asynchronous arrivals, delayed load reports, and engine-local memory
management in production clusters, we translate these principles into a practical controller named PARK,
which pairs online projected subgradient price updates and one-turn migration lookahead with a local KV
retention index ranked by expected reuse value per byte-epoch. In real GPU cluster experiments serving a
197-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model on multi-turn software-engineering agent benchmarks (SWE
and Terminal-Bench), PARK outperforms all five load-balancing and prefix-aware baselines across contrasting
traffic regimes. On 16 H200 GPUs, PARK raises output throughput by 24.2% over the strongest baseline
(336.9% over round robin) on turn-intensive SWE trajectories and by 40.0% over the strongest baseline
(63.3% over round robin) on generation-intensive Terminal-Bench trajectories. Controlled single-replica
ablations show that our retention index alone cuts prior-prefix token loss from 13.26% to 2.17% and increases
throughput by 36.7% over least-recently-used (LRU) eviction, while 128-GPU scale-up experiments sustain
50,789 to 67,363 output tokens/s across 16 replicas with prefix cache hit rates of 91.3% to 97.4%.
Keywords: multi-turn LLM inference, KV cache retention, online resource allocation, fluid approximation
∗The co-first authors contributed equally to this work and are listed in alphabetical order.
† Corresponding author.

1. Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) support a growing range of activities, including customer service,
writing, software development, and tool-using AI agents. Delivering these benefits requires inference:
the computation performed by a trained model to generate a response to a user’s request. Whereas
training develops a model’s capabilities once, inference puts those capabilities to use each time a
request is served, consuming processing capacity, memory, and energy on graphics processing units
(GPUs). Inference is therefore a recurring operating requirement with substantial costs: OpenAI
reportedly spent $8.4 billion on inference in 2025 (Muppidi, 2026), and McKinsey & Company
(2026) projects that inference will account for about 60% of AI data-center demand by 2030. At
this scale, modest reductions in the resources required per request can yield substantial operating
savings or allow existing infrastructure to serve more demand. Realizing these gains poses a natural
operations research problem: how can a provider complete more useful work with limited resources
and uncertain demand?
We study a provider operating multiple inference servers, each of which may contain several GPUs.
Requests arrive sequentially, and the provider must immediately decide whether to admit each
request and which server should process it. Admitted requests occupy computation and memory
resources while their responses are generated, sharing those resources with unfinished work from
earlier admissions. Memory is particularly important because generating a response requires storing
intermediate computations whose size grows with the amount of text being processed (Kwon et al.,
2023).
This allocation problem is further complicated because many requests belong to multi-turn
conversations, where each turn consists of a prompt and its response. A later prompt builds on
the conversation’s earlier text, creating an opportunity to reuse previous computation. The saved
intermediate computations are called the key–value (KV) cache. Keeping this cache reduces the
work required for the next turn, but occupies GPU memory while the user reads a response or
executes external tools. Therefore, the provider must also decide which idle conversations deserve
continued storage and which caches to evict, meaning remove from memory. Eviction frees capacity
for other work, at the cost of rebuilding the lost computations if the conversation resumes.
Crucially, request routing and cache eviction are closely coupled in multi-turn conversations.
Serving a turn creates an updated cache at the chosen server, while eviction determines whether
that cache remains available to reduce the cost of subsequent requests. Consider a conversation
whose cache resides at a busy server while another server has spare capacity. Routing the next
request to the cache-holding server avoids recomputation but adds to its load; routing it to the other
server uses spare capacity and establishes an updated cache there, but requires rebuilding the prefix.
Whether routing elsewhere is preferable depends on how long the destination’s congestion advantage


--- Page 3 ---
3
persists and how likely the conversation is to continue. The eviction decision, in turn, determines
which idle caches to retain by weighing the memory freed by eviction against the potential savings
from future reuse. A retained cache occupies memory that could support other requests and saves
computation only if the next request arrives before eviction and is routed to the server holding it.
Existing inference systems demonstrate the practical value of preserving caches across conversation
turns (Gao et al., 2024) and coordinating distributed routing to balance cache reuse and server
load (Srivatsa et al., 2025). Related optimization studies develop bid-price admission and routing
in a single-turn model under resource constraints (Chen et al., 2026) and cache eviction policies for
stochastic multi-turn conversations (Zhang et al., 2025). These developments motivate a unified
optimization and analysis of routing and cache retention. As the preceding discussion illustrates,
the central challenge is to coordinate these decisions while accounting for how each shapes the costs
and benefits of the other across conversation turns. We therefore ask:
How should a scheduler jointly optimize admission, routing, and idle-cache retention to
maximize the throughput under server-specific computation and memory constraints?
We formulate this problem as a stochastic control model and develop a tractable fluid relaxation
that links active service, idle waiting, and cache ownership across conversation turns. Resource
shadow prices and session continuation values provide a common basis for coordinating these
decisions, yielding structural characterizations of optimal fluid routing and retention. We further
develop a fluid-based policy with an asymptotic performance guarantee and translate the theoretical
principles into PARK, a practical controller for multi-turn inference. Our main contributions are as
follows.
• A fluid framework for jointly managing service and future cache reuse. We formulate a
stochastic control model for admission, routing, and cache retention in multi-turn conversations
that tracks each session’s service status, idle age, and cache location. Because continuous
relaxations of routing and retention fractions yield nonlinear capacity constraints, we develop
a fluid approximation expressed through state–action flow volumes. This formulation yields a
tractable linear program while preserving the link between current service and future cache
availability.
• Structural characterization of routing and cache eviction. The fluid solution provides
a common economic basis for evaluating routing and retention decisions: dual resource prices
measure the cost of computation and memory, while continuation values capture the conse-
quences for later turns. Their comparison explains when routing should follow an existing cache
and when rebuilding it elsewhere is worthwhile. For retention, we derive sufficient conditions
connecting cache length, storage cost, and the conditional time until the next prompt. These
conditions show why intermediate-length caches can offer a better trade-off than short caches


--- Page 4 ---
4
(which are cheap to rebuild) or very long caches (which occupy more memory than their future
reuse justifies), and characterize how idle age should govern eviction through the session’s
return prospect and rebuild cost, yielding a mechanism distinct from that of the traditional
LRU policy.
• A fluid-based policy with an asymptotic performance guarantee. We turn the fluid
solution into an online buffer-reserve policy that makes immediate routing decisions and
periodically updates its admission and cache-retention quotas while reserving capacity buffers
against stochastic fluctuations. Letting arrival rates and server capacities grow proportionally
with a scale parameter n, we prove an O(√nlog n) shortfall in expected completed turns
relative to the fluid benchmark. Thus, the shortfall per unit of scale vanishes, providing a
performance guarantee in large stochastic systems.
• A practical controller (PARK) informed by the theory and evaluated at scale. To
handle asynchronous arrivals, delayed server snapshots, and engine-local memory reclamation
in production clusters, we translate our routing and retention principles into an event-driven
controller, PARK (Price-based Admission and Routing with KV-cache Retention). We evaluate
PARK on two multi-turn software-engineering agent workloads, serving a 197-billion-parameter
mixture-of-experts model on up to 128 H200 GPUs with a concurrency cap of 4,096 sessions.
In three-hour evaluations at this scale, PARK sustains approximately 51,000–67,000 output
tokens/s across the two workloads. PARK outperforms standard routing and caching baselines,
while controlled single-replica experiments show that its retention index mechanism reduces
prior-prefix token loss from 13.26% to 2.17%.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the related literature.
Section 3 introduces the stochastic model. Section 4 develops the fluid formulation and structural
results. Section 5 presents the policy, its performance guarantee, and its implementation. Section 6
reports the experiments, and Section 7 concludes. Proofs appear in the electronic companion.
2. Related Literature
Our work relates to three streams of research: LLM inference systems and cache management,
optimization for LLM inference, and dynamic resource allocation.
LLM inference systems and cache management. Modern serving engines improve GPU
memory efficiency and reuse earlier computations across calls. PagedAttention reduces KV-cache
fragmentation and enables memory sharing (Kwon et al., 2023), SGLang reuses shared prompt
prefixes across calls (Zheng et al., 2024), CachedAttention preserves multi-turn KV caches across
a storage hierarchy (Gao et al., 2024), and Preble coordinates distributed routing to balance
cache locality and server load (Srivatsa et al., 2025). While these systems establish the practical


--- Page 5 ---
5
importance of cache reuse, we provide a unified theoretical framework that jointly prices current
resource use and future conversation turns, explaining when routing and eviction should depart
from myopic heuristics.
Classical caching models also study retention decisions: Dehghan et al. (2016) optimize content-
specific cache utilities, and Ferragut et al. (2016) link optimal time-to-live timers to inter-request
time distributions. In multi-turn LLM inference, however, idle caches compete directly with active
requests for GPU memory, and reuse value depends on whether and where future turns are admitted.
Our retention comparisons incorporate these service decisions to characterize how cache length, idle
age, and return timing govern eviction.
Optimization and stochastic control for LLM inference. Recent work builds mathematical
foundations for inference scheduling. Mitzenmacher and Shahout (2025) survey connections among
queueing, service-time predictions, and LLM serving. Dai et al. (2026) establish throughput
optimality in batched processing networks, including dependent AI-agent workflows. Ao et al.
(2026) develop fluid-guided admission and scheduling policies accounting for KV-memory growth
during generation, while Lin et al. (2026) derive asymptotically optimal admission and routing
policies for competing prompt and generation stages. Related studies examine online batching under
KV-memory limits (Jaillet et al., 2026), non-clairvoyant scheduling without advance output lengths
(Feng et al., 2026), and cache-aware preemption for tail latency (Li et al., 2026).
Two closely related studies address routing and eviction separately: Chen et al. (2026) develop
online bid-price routing in a single-turn model under concurrent-request and KV-memory limits, and
Zhang et al. (2025) propose a length-aware variant of least-recently-used eviction that is optimal for
a tail-latency objective under a stochastic model of multi-turn conversations. Wu et al. (2026) model
routing–eviction interactions, but their routing algorithm greedily minimizes predicted latency for
the current request, and their competitive guarantees apply to eviction rather than the combined
policy. In contrast, our fluid framework jointly optimizes admission, routing, and retention across
conversation turns: routing determines where future caches reside, while retention governs the
cost of future routing choices. By accounting for these intertemporal effects, our framework yields
structural characterizations of the joint decisions and an asymptotic optimality guarantee for our
buffer-reserve policy.
Dynamic resource allocation. Methodologically, our approach builds on bid-price control
(Talluri and van Ryzin, 1998) and fluid reoptimization (Jasin and Kumar, 2012; Bumpensanti and
Wang, 2020). Reusable-resource models track capacity occupied for stochastic service durations and
released upon completion (Goyal et al., 2025). Multi-turn inference adds a post-service state effect:
completing a turn can leave behind a cache that continues to consume memory while reducing
future execution work, both of which our routing and retention rules price.


--- Page 6 ---
6
Our state-based LP also connects to weakly coupled Markov decision processes, where local session
dynamics share global capacity constraints (Adelman and Mersereau, 2008; Bertsimas and Miˇsi´c,
2016). In this literature, Brown and Zhang (2022) incorporate shared external signals, and Brown
and Zhang (2025) and Gast et al. (2024) establish finite-horizon asymptotic optimality guarantees
for fluid reoptimization with heterogeneous components. Building on these ideas, we link session
states across turns to connect resource shadow prices with cache-ownership values, accommodating
immediate routing, random service requirements, and post-service retention decisions to achieve an
O(√nlog n) shortfall from the fluid benchmark.
3. Model and Decision Problem
3.1. Sessions, Endpoints, and Cache States
We consider a discrete-time LLM inference system operating over a finite horizon of H epochs,
indexed by t = 0,...,H −1, with terminal time H. The system serves conversation sessions across a
set of endpoints E = {1,...,E}, where each endpoint represents a server housing one or more GPUs
(processors used for LLM computation) with per-epoch execution capacity Be and memory capacity
Ge. Upon arrival, each prompt must be immediately assigned to an endpoint or rejected; we write
E0 = {0} ∪E, where action 0 denotes rejection. After a rejection, the session may depart or remain
idle without a cache, in which case it may submit a new prompt or retry the rejected one in a later
epoch.
We call a submitted prompt a request. Each session consists of a sequence of turns, where a
turn comprises an admitted request and its generated response. Each completed request therefore
corresponds to one completed turn. Serving a turn involves processing the prompt and generating
the response, which may span multiple epochs. A session is active while its admitted turn is
unfinished and idle while waiting to submit another prompt. After a turn completes, its key–value
(KV) cache stores intermediate computations that can be reused by a later turn. Retaining an idle
cache consumes endpoint memory between turns but reduces computation when the session returns.
Each idle session has at most one retained cache: routing its next prompt to the endpoint holding
that cache is a warm route, whereas routing elsewhere, or routing without a retained cache, is a
cold route that requires recomputation.
Each live session has a state s = (k,a,d,o,x) in a finite set S (departed sessions are excluded),
where:
• k records the session type or conversation phase, such as its context length, number of completed
turns, or idle cache size;
• a is the idle age (number of epochs elapsed since the previous turn completed), with a = 0 for
active sessions;


--- Page 7 ---
7
• d is the attained service (number of epochs spent serving the unfinished turn), with d = 0 for
idle sessions;
• o ∈E0 is the endpoint holding an idle session’s retained cache, with o = 0 indicating no retained
cache;
• x ∈E0 is the endpoint serving an unfinished turn, with x = 0 for idle sessions.
Together, these coordinates capture all workload information needed to determine service require-
ments and return behavior. We partition S = SI ˙∪SA into idle states (SI, where d = x = 0) and
active states (SA, where a = 0); the cache-location coordinate o is relevant only in SI.
Finally, let Ms(t) be the number of sessions in state s at the beginning of epoch t, and write
M(t) = (Ms(t))s∈S. When a turn completes at endpoint e, a continuing session becomes idle with
its updated cache stored at e. Thus, the current routing decision directly determines where the
next turn can reuse earlier computations.
3.2. Decisions and Session Dynamics
In each epoch t, decisions and state transitions occur in four steps:
(1) Observe the population. The controller observes M(t), including the serving endpoints of
active sessions and the cache locations of idle sessions.
(2) Route each arriving prompt. Each beginning-of-epoch idle session in state s independently
submits a prompt with probability ps(t), while new sessions may enter with an initial prompt
and no retained cache. Active sessions submit no prompts, so every session submits at most
one prompt per epoch. Arrival times and new-session counts follow specified distributions,
with new-session arrivals bounded per epoch.
Indexing arrivals by j = 1,...,Jt with session states st,j, the controller immediately chooses
an action et,j ∈E0 upon each arrival, using all information observed up to that moment
(including earlier arrivals and routing decisions in epoch t). Assigning et,j ∈E admits the
prompt to endpoint et,j, where it remains until completion; action 0 rejects it.
(3) Observe service outcomes at the boundary. Previously active and newly admitted turns
receive service, yielding pre-retention states esi(t + 1) at the epoch boundary according to three
state–action transition kernels:
• QA
t (s,s′) for an initially active session;
• QI
t(s,s′) for an idle session that submits no prompt;
• P e
t (s,s′) for an arriving session assigned action e ∈E0.
Here s′ denotes the pre-retention state, and any probability mass unassigned to live states
corresponds to session departure. Specifically, an unfinished turn remains active with attained
service d′ = d + 1; a completed turn either departs or becomes idle at its serving endpoint e


--- Page 8 ---
8
with (a′,d′,x′,o′) = (0,0,0,e); an unprompted idle session remains idle with age a′ = a + 1; and
a rejected prompt releases any existing cache without starting service. Conditional on the
beginning-of-epoch state and arrival sequence, transition and resource outcomes are independent
across sessions and depend only on each session’s current state and action, though computation,
memory use, and completion may be correlated within a session.
(4) Retain caches and update the population. Let eIe(t) be the set of idle sessions with
a cache available at endpoint e at the boundary (including newly completed turns). After
observing service outcomes and cache sizes, the controller selects a subset Ie(t) ⊆eIe(t) to retain
and evicts the rest. Eviction clears only the cache location via E(k,a,0,o,0) = (k,a,0,0,0)
without altering user conversation behavior. Post-retention states and the next population are

3.3. Capacity Constraints and Optimization
Let At be the set of active sessions at the beginning of epoch t. During epoch t, an initially active
session i ∈At incurs execution requirement Lt,i,e at endpoint e (with Lt,i,e = 0 if served elsewhere),
and arrival j incurs execution requirement Ct,j,e if admitted to endpoint e. We enforce memory
capacity at epoch boundaries as a discrete-time approximation: an initially active turn and a newly
admitted turn occupy boundary memory Kact

through their retained idle caches of observed size bi(t).
All per-session execution requirements and active-memory footprints are nonnegative and uni-
formly bounded. Conditional on the beginning-of-epoch state and arrival sequence, these random
quantities are independent across sessions and follow known distributions determined by each
session’s state and action, though their realizations are unknown at the time of routing.

only the information observed up to each decision time. Letting N cmp(t) denote the number of turns

Maximizing completions is therefore equivalent to maximizing admissions minus the unfinished
turns remaining at the terminal time H.
Solving (3.1) requires trading off immediate service against future cache reuse: routing determines
where subsequent turns can reuse computations, while retention determines whether those caches
remain available. Because these decisions interact across sessions through shared computation
and memory limits, exact dynamic programming is intractable. The next section develops a fluid
approximation that preserves these intertemporal interactions and leads to a tractable policy.
Remark 3.1 (Emergency intervention). The formulation in (3.1) describes normal operation. For
theoretical analysis, we assume that a causal emergency rule can halt admissions and interrupt
active turns before any endpoint exceeds capacity, with interrupted turns earning no completion
reward. This rule serves solely to keep the policy well defined on exceptional sample paths and is
not intended for practical implementation; our policy reserves capacity to make such interventions
rare, and we bound their impact on performance separately.


--- Page 10 ---
10
4. The Fluid Approximation and Structural Insights
We develop a fluid approximation to characterize how anticipated cache reuse should govern current
admission, routing, and retention decisions. Routing a turn determines where a conversation’s
history can next be reused, whereas retention determines whether that history survives until the
conversation returns. Theorem 4.1 couples these decisions through endpoint-specific shadow prices
for computation and memory together with each conversation’s continuation value.
For routing, the fluid model favors the endpoint with the highest bid, combining the value
of serving the current turn, the cost of the resources it consumes, and the resulting change in
continuation value. When endpoints face similar congestion, keeping a conversation at its cached
endpoint avoids rebuilding its prefix. By contrast, a persistent congestion imbalance can justify
migrating a conversation even when doing so makes the current turn more expensive: the rebuild
penalty is incurred once, whereas lower congestion yields recurring savings over subsequent turns.
Consequently, two conversations facing the same load imbalance may warrant different routes
depending on their remaining turn horizons.
For retention, the fluid model preserves an idle cache whenever the continuation value it protects
exceeds the one-epoch opportunity cost of the memory it occupies. This trade-off explains why
intermediate-length prefixes can deserve priority: short prefixes are inexpensive to rebuild, whereas
very long prefixes may consume more memory than a conversation’s remaining turns can justify.
Return timing matters as well: when tool execution takes a predictable amount of time, a session
that has already been idle for several epochs may be the closest to returning.
These structural insights directly guide the design of the practical algorithm PARK in Section 5.3
later. Its admission and routing controller updates resource prices online and approximates the
continuation benefit of migration by comparing the cost of one subsequent warm turn across
endpoints. Meanwhile, its cache manager ranks idle prefixes by their estimated reuse benefit per
unit of memory and time, accounting for both prefix length and the effective waiting time per
successful reuse.
4.1. The Fluid Linear Program
Replacing random quantities with their expectations and discrete decisions with continuous fractions
does not immediately yield a linear program. To see why, let ms(t) denote the fluid population
in state s (with ms(0) = M 0
s ), and let αs,e(t) be the fraction of arriving state-s prompts routed
to endpoint e. The resulting execution load is cs,e(t)

a state-s prompt admitted to e. Because both the future population ms(t) and the routing fraction

αs,e(t) depend on policy decisions, their product is bilinear. An analogous nonlinearity arises when
multiplying the post-service idle population by the fraction of caches retained.
To restore linearity, we instead optimize directly over state–action flow volumes: the total mass
of prompts routed and caches retained in each state. This reformulation makes both resource
consumption and population dynamics linear while preserving how current decisions govern future
cache availability. We first present the resulting linear program, and then use its dual prices to
derive routing and retention principles that account for a conversation’s future turns.

τ = t,...,H −1,
m, em,y,z ≥0.
(4.7)
Total fluid completions equal NA(M) + Vt(M), and setting t = 0 and M = M 0 recovers the initial
planning problem.
This linear program links current routing and retention decisions to future service requirements
through the evolving distribution of cache locations. Its dual shadow prices allow us to weigh the
immediate resource cost of each action against the continuation value of the session state it creates,
and we formalize this comparison next to derive routing and retention principles.
4.2. Bid Prices and the Value of Future Cache Reuse
Fix a feasible remaining-horizon LP (4.7) starting at epoch t0 with population M, and let

The next theorem characterizes optimal fluid routing and retention decisions in terms of these

Theorem 4.1 (Optimal routing and retention rules). For any optimal fluid solution and the dual
prices above:
a. A positive routing flow ys,e(t) > 0 uses an action maximizing Bs,e(t) over E0.
b. For a cached idle state with positive pre-retention population, its cache is retained if ∆s(t+1) >
γo(s)(t)bs and evicted if the inequality is reversed.

--- Page 14 ---
14
Thus, routing to e1 rather than e2 is optimal whenever its continuation-value advantage outweighs
any higher immediate resource cost.
Suppose endpoint e2 holds the session’s cache. When shadow prices and future service conditions
are similar across endpoints, cache reuse lowers cs,e2(t) and makes e2 cheaper to use, favoring warm
routing. However, if e2 becomes sufficiently congested, its higher shadow prices raise rs,e2(t) and
depress future continuation values there, making migration to a less loaded endpoint e1 worthwhile
despite the upfront cost of rebuilding the cache. This trade-off mirrors the intuition behind SGLang’s
cache aware routing rule SGLang (2026), which prioritizes cache locality when server loads are
balanced but switches to the least-loaded endpoint once load imbalance exceeds a threshold.
Condition (4.11) also highlights the role of remaining conversation length. Serving the current turn
at e1 establishes a warm cache there for subsequent turns; if e1 is expected to remain less congested,
those future turns yield recurring savings that amortize the one-time rebuild cost. Migration is
therefore attractive for a conversation with many turns remaining, whereas it will not pay off for a
session nearing completion. Consequently, the congestion gap needed to justify rerouting depends
jointly on expected remaining turns, the persistence of the destination’s cost advantage, and the
memory price of retaining the newly built cache.
While routing determines where the next cache is created, retention determines whether it remains
available for reuse. The next subsection uses Theorem 4.1.b to examine how cache length, idle age,
and return timing govern which caches should be retained.
4.3. Which Idle Caches Should Be Retained?
An idle cache occupies memory now to save computation when the next prompt arrives. Theo-
rem 4.1.b compares this future benefit against the boundary memory charge: retain the cache
when ∆s(t + 1) > γo(s)(t)bs, and evict it when the inequality is reversed. We use this comparison to
examine how cache length, return timing, and idle age govern the value of retaining an idle cache.
Fix an idle cache at endpoint e at the boundary ending epoch t, with prefix length L > 0 and
memory footprint bs = βL (β > 0). There are N = H −t −1 ≥1 remaining prompt epochs. Let T
denote the number of epochs until the next prompt, with T = ∞if the session does not return
within the horizon. For tractability, suppose the endpoint’s memory shadow price remains constant
at γ > 0 across waiting boundaries; Appendix EC.1.3 provides exact conditions and extends the
analysis to time-varying prices.
The cost of waiting for reuse. Suppose we retain the cache for at most u epochs, evicting it if
no prompt arrives by then. Over this waiting window, the expected storage duration is E[min(T,u)]


--- Page 15 ---
15
and the probability of reusing the cache before eviction is P(T ≤u). Define the effective waiting
time per cached return by
deff =
min
1≤u≤N
P(T ≤u)>0
E[min(T,u)]
P(T ≤u)
,
(4.12)
with deff = ∞when no return is possible (in which case immediate eviction is optimal). Thus,
deff measures the minimum expected storage time per successful cache reuse across all stopping
deadlines u. For example, if a prompt arrives deterministically in five epochs, then deff = 5, so
retaining the cache can be optimal even when an immediate return in the next epoch has probability
zero. For random return times, deff incorporates the option to abandon waiting early and therefore
differs from the unconditional mean E[T].
Conditions for keeping or evicting a cache. For a session with a positive probability of
return, let R < ∞uniformly bound its expected remaining completions under any admissible policy,
conditional on the history and chosen route at a cached return or at the first cold admission
after eviction. Suppose further that, following eviction, the first cold admission incurs an expected
execution charge of at least
λ(a1L + a2L2),
a1 ≥0,
a2 > 0,
λ ≥0,
(4.13)
where λ lower-bounds the execution shadow price and the linear and quadratic terms capture the
computation required to rebuild the lost prefix (see, e.g., Vaswani et al. 2017; Hoffmann et al. 2022).
When the session instead returns with its cache intact, its continuation value equals expected future
completions minus future execution and memory charges; let ε(L) uniformly bound how far this
value falls below R across all feasible return dates. A smaller ε(L) thus indicates that retaining the
cache preserves more of the session’s potential completion value (Appendix EC.1.3.1 formalizes
ε(L) and provides explicit upper bounds).
The following proposition establishes sufficient conditions for fluid retention and eviction, showing
how cache length and return timing jointly govern eviction; its proof appears in Appendix EC.1.3.2.
Proposition 4.2. Under the preceding setting, the following are sufficient conditions for the fluid
retention decision.
• For long cache,
γbsdeff > R
=⇒
evict.
(4.14)
• For cache with intermediate length,
γbsdeff + ε(L) < min{λ(a1L + a2L2),R}
=⇒
retain.
(4.15)
• For short cache, additionally suppose that, under each fixed routing action, cache reuse changes
only execution cost, with savings at most ¯λe(a1L + a2L2), where ¯λe ≥0. Then
¯λe(a1 + a2L) < βγdeff
=⇒
evict.
(4.16)


--- Page 16 ---
16
Condition (4.15) compares the minimum storage cost per cached return against a lower bound
on the net value preserved by the cache, whereas (4.14) and (4.16) reverse this comparison using
upper bounds on that benefit. Proposition 4.2 yields three structural implications.
Why intermediate lengths can be worth protecting.
• Short caches save too little computation. When prefix-recomputation savings are primarily
quadratic in length (a1 ≈0), reuse savings shrink faster than linear storage costs as L decreases.
Under the additional service assumption, (4.16) implies that sufficiently short caches are
cheaper to rebuild than to retain, holding return prospects and shadow prices fixed.
• Very long caches consume too much memory. By (4.14), retaining a cache is subopti-
mal whenever L > R/(βγdeff). Even a costly rebuild cannot justify storage if the remaining
conversation offers too few expected completions R to amortize the memory rent.
• Intermediate-length caches merit highest retention priority. Caches of moderate length
are expensive enough to rebuild yet compact enough to store profitably. Appendix EC.1.3.3
derives an explicit interval of protected cache lengths under simple service-cost bounds.
How waiting for reuse affects retention. Cache value also depends on how long memory
must be held before the next prompt arrives. Holding cache length, continuation bounds, and
shadow prices fixed, a larger deff increases the storage cost per return, tightening the retention
condition (4.15) and relaxing the eviction conditions (4.14)–(4.16). In particular, the maximum
justifiable cache length R/(βγdeff) shrinks as deff grows, so even a cache that is expensive to rebuild
should be evicted if capturing its reuse requires excessive waiting.
When idle age is a useful guide. An older cache is not automatically less valuable; what
matters is what its idle age reveals about the residual time until the next prompt. For a given
session class, let U denote the total idle duration (in epochs) from the previous turn’s completion
to the next prompt, possibly infinite. For a session already idle for a epochs, define its conditional
return probability (hazard rate) in the next epoch by
p(a,L) = P(U = a + 1 | U > a,L).
The following corollary characterizes how the effective waiting time deff(a,L) varies with a session’s
idle age a under decreasing, increasing, and constant return-probability regimes.
Corollary 4.3. Compare idle ages at a fixed cache length and remaining horizon. If p(a,L) is
nonincreasing in a, then
deff(a,L) = 1/p(a,L),
with 1/0 = ∞, and deff is nondecreasing in age. If p(a,L) is nondecreasing in a, then deff is
nonincreasing in age. If p(a,L) is constant in a, then deff is independent of age.


--- Page 17 ---
17
Because a larger deff favors eviction, Corollary 4.3 explains when least-recently-used (LRU; see,
e.g., Mattson et al. 1970; Zheng et al. 2024) eviction is effective and when it fails. When the return
hazard p(a,L) decreases with idle age, meaning longer inactivity signals a less imminent return, deff
increases with a, making LRU sensible. Conversely, when a prompt is expected after a bounded
processing or tool-execution delay, the return hazard increases with age: an older session is closer
to returning, so LRU can prematurely evict a cache that is about to be reused. Combining cache
length with return-time behavior therefore provides a sharper eviction criterion than recency alone.
The routing and retention principles developed in this section characterize optimal decisions in the
deterministic fluid model. Implementing these insights in a stochastic system requires safeguarding
against random fluctuations in arrivals, service durations, and memory footprints. The next section
introduces a buffer-reserve policy that translates the fluid solution into online decisions and proves
that its performance loss relative to the fluid benchmark grows sublinearly with system scale.
5. A Fluid-Based Policy: Theory and Implementation
In this section, we first present a buffer-reserve policy that implements the fluid solution and
establish its asymptotic performance guarantee, and we then adapt its decision rules for practical
cluster deployment. The buffer-reserve policy inherits the fluid model’s bid-price structure. For
routing, an endpoint’s bid weighs the value of serving a turn, including future cache reuse, against
its shadow cost of computation and memory. For retention, an idle cache is kept whenever its
continuation benefit exceeds the shadow cost of the memory it occupies. Building on this logic, our
practical algorithm, PARK (described in Section 5.3), approximates these comparisons using online
resource prices and a one-turn lookahead for admission and routing, alongside an index of expected
reuse benefit per unit of memory and time for cache retention.
5.1. The Buffer-Reserve Policy
The fluid LP plans resource allocation using conditional expectations, whereas actual arrivals,
execution requirements, and memory footprints fluctuate around their means. Allocating full
nominal capacity can therefore trigger an overload within the current epoch that re-solving at the
next epoch cannot undo. Multi-turn service compounds this risk across epochs: unfinished turns
carry inherited resource commitments into future epochs that cannot be shed by rejecting new
prompts, while random completions govern when and where idle caches appear. To guard against
both within-epoch spikes and multi-turn population drift, we pair progressive capacity reserves
with epoch-by-epoch reoptimization.
Fix a reserve parameter r > 0. When solving the fluid LP at epoch t, we reduce the available
capacities at each remaining epoch τ to
B−,t
e
(τ) = Be −(τ −t + 1)r,
G−,t
e (τ) = Ge −(τ −t + 1)r,
τ = t,...,H −1.
(5.1)


--- Page 18 ---
18
Algorithm 1 Buffer-reserve fluid policy
At each epoch t, until an emergency occurs:
1. Plan. Solve (4.7) from M(t) with capacities (5.1). If infeasible, invoke the emergency rule.
Otherwise, select an optimal solution via a fixed deterministic tie-breaking rule, and denote its
current-epoch flows by ys,e(t) and zs,K(t).
2. Route. Upon arrival j in state st,j, assign et,j = e to the first endpoint e ∈E in a fixed state-
specific order that has remaining quota:
j−1
X
i=1
1{st,i = st,j, et,i = e} < ⌊yst,j,e(t)⌋.
If no such endpoint exists, reject the prompt (et,j = 0). Unused quotas expire at the epoch
boundary.
3. Retain. Observe the pre-retention states esi(t + 1), including newly completed sessions. For each
idle state s with o(s) = e̸ = 0, retain ⌊zs,K(t)⌋caches (or all available caches if fewer exist) in a
fixed session order, forming Ie(t). Evict all remaining idle caches, update M(t + 1), and proceed
to epoch t + 1.
Thus, epoch t holds back r units of each resource, and the buffer grows linearly across future
epochs. When the LP is re-solved at t + 1 from the observed population M(t + 1), each future
epoch τ ≥t + 1 regains r units of capacity relative to the previous plan. This released slack ensures
recourse feasibility when realized populations, particularly ongoing active turns, exceed their fluid
predictions, while reoptimization adapts routing and retention quotas to realized cache locations.
Algorithm 1 converts the current-epoch fluid flows into rounded integer quotas, making immediate
routing decisions upon arrival and boundary retention decisions after service outcomes are observed.
Whenever a capacity intervention is required or the re-solved LP becomes infeasible, the causal
emergency rule from Section 3 applies.
Connection to bid-price control. By Theorem 4.1, positive flows in the buffered LP follow the
optimal bid-price routing and retention comparisons under the buffered dual prices, while the flow
magnitudes resolve ties among indifferent actions and enforce capacity limits. Algorithm 1 implements
these primal–dual decisions through rounded quotas that are refreshed at every reoptimization.

transitions contribute O(√n), the capacity reserve rn sacrifices O(√nlog n), and rare emergency
interventions contribute O(1/n). Setting rn = b√nlog n balances these effects: it provides enough
slack at each reoptimization to absorb drift in unfinished work and preserve LP feasibility with
high probability, while adapting routing and retention quotas to realized cache locations.
Remark 5.3 (Asymptotic optimality). Theorem 5.2 can also yield an asymptotic optimality guarantee
when all policies have access to the same emergency rule. For this comparison, we charge each
policy a fixed penalty per interrupted turn, large enough to cover the benefit of freeing capacity.
The emergency rule is a theoretical safeguard: the buffer-reserve policy reserves enough capacity
that it needs to interrupt service only on rare sample paths. Its expected total penalty therefore
vanishes as the system grows, and its expected completions net of penalties are within O(√nlog n)
of the best feasible policy. Appendix EC.2 gives the proof.
5.3. Practical Implementation: Asynchronous Primal–Dual Control and Index Eviction
The buffer-reserve policy (Algorithm 1) operates in synchronous epochs, observes the full system
state before each decision, re-solves a multi-epoch linear program at every step, and directly enforces
both routing and cache eviction. While these abstractions facilitate theoretical analysis, production
LLM serving clusters differ in three operational respects:
(i) Asynchronous arrivals and delayed state updates: Prompts arrive continuously between control
updates, while endpoint utilization snapshots arrive with delay, making it computationally
prohibitive to re-solve a multi-epoch LP at every arrival.
(ii) Decoupled admission and dispatch: Because routing decisions precede actual client dispatch,
the controller must reserve capacity through short-lived admission offers to prevent concurrent
requests from double-booking resources.
(iii) Engine-local cache reclamation: In production inference engines (such as vLLM; see, e.g., vLLM
2026), the central router does not forcibly evict KV blocks; instead, each endpoint’s local
memory manager reclaims unpinned idle blocks on demand whenever active generation requires
space.


--- Page 21 ---
21

To bridge these gaps while preserving the economic structure of Theorem 4.1 and Algorithm 1,
we pair an event-driven admission and routing controller (approximating the bid-price rule in
Theorem 4.1.a) with an endpoint-local retention index (approximating the retention rule in Theo-
rem 4.1.b). Rather than re-solving the full fluid LP, the central controller maintains shadow prices
λe ≥0 for computation and γe ≥0 for active memory at each endpoint e ∈E, uses them to evaluate
bid scores, and updates them via projected subgradient steps on excess desired demand. Simul-
taneously, each endpoint ranks reclaimable idle caches using a Gittins-style value-per-byte-epoch
index derived from Section 4.3. We refer to the resulting integrated policy as PARK (summarized
in Algorithm 2), with experimental parameter values listed in Table EC.1, and full implementation
details included in Section EC.3.2, both in the Appendix. Table 1 contrasts how PARK and the
buffer-reserve policy translate the two bid-price comparisons of Theorem 4.1 into serving decisions.
Admission and routing. For a ready request i and endpoint e, let wie denote the estimated
computation work for the uncached prompt and generated reply, and let mie denote the estimated
active KV-memory footprint. For a returning session, the controller credits expected prefix reuse
only at its current cache owner oi. It assigns endpoint e the bid score
sie = 1 + ωi −λewie −γemie + ∆ie.
(5.5)
Here, 1 represents the unit reward for serving the turn, ωi is a bounded bonus that increases
with waiting time prior to admission, and λe and γe price computation work and active memory,
respectively. For a new session or a return to the current owner, ∆ie = 0. For a migration away from
the owner, ∆ie = α(Fioi −Fie), where Fie is the priced resource cost of serving one subsequent warm
turn at endpoint e and α is a lookahead weight. Thus, migrating a session incurs the immediate
cost of rebuilding its prefix, but earns credit for lower congestion on the next turn.


--- Page 22 ---
22
The controller restricts eligibility to endpoints with recent status reports. A returning session
may migrate only when the candidate destination exhibits a sustained load advantage, offers a
sufficiently higher bid than the current owner, and has elapsed a minimum cooldown since its
previous endpoint binding. Standard requests are processed in decreasing order of their best eligible
bid: each receives an offer for its highest-bidding eligible route that has a nonnegative bid and
sufficient residual capacity after accounting for ongoing work and outstanding offers, while unplaced
requests remain held in queue. Overdue requests are processed first in arrival order and may bypass
the bid nonnegativity check, subject to the same capacity limits.
Updating prices. For each resource j (computation work or active memory), let Cej denote
the capacity budget at endpoint e and Dej its desired load, comprising ongoing work, outstanding
offers, and the demand of every ready request whose best eligible bid is nonnegative and selects
e, which is measured before capacity checks. Writing pej for the unit shadow price (λe or γe) and
zej = Cejpej for its budget-scaled value, the controller updates prices with step size η > 0 via
z+
ej =

zej + η(Dej/Cej −1)

+.
(5.6)
Measuring desired demand prior to capacity filtering allows an endpoint’s shadow price to keep
rising even after its admissions are capped.
KV cache retention and eviction. For an idle prefix of length L and idle age a, let bs = βL
denote its memory footprint and c
deff(a,L) the estimated holding time per successful reuse, as
defined in (4.12). Each endpoint evaluates the retention index
bI(L,a) =
bg(L,a)
bs c
deff(a,L)
,
bg(L,a) = min{ bR, λe(a1L + a2L2)}.
(5.7)
The numerator prices the work saved upon reuse at the estimated execution shadow price λe, using
linear and quadratic rebuild-cost coefficients a1 and a2, and caps the resulting benefit at a fixed
reference value; the index is set to zero if no useful return is forecast. Because the memory allocator
reclaims physical KV blocks rather than whole sessions, it quantizes each session’s index into a
discrete priority and sums those priorities across all sessions sharing a given block. Unpinned,
reclaimable blocks are bucketed by aggregate priority and evicted from the lowest nonempty bucket
first, allowing shared prefix blocks to survive eviction even when individual sharing sessions have
modest standalone priority.
6. Experimental Results
We evaluate our framework using real multi-turn AI-agent workloads on large-scale GPU clusters.
Section 6.1 describes the experimental environment, workload characteristics, benchmark policies,
and performance metrics. Section 6.2 compares PARK (Algorithm 2) against standard routing
and caching baselines across 16- and 128-GPU deployments. Finally, Section 6.3 isolates the two
mechanisms driving these gains: value-aware cache retention and session-affine routing.


--- Page 23 ---
23
Algorithm 2 PARK (Price-based Admission and Routing with KV-cache Retention)
Central controller, each control round.
1. Refresh endpoint loads and outstanding offers, and estimate the work and active memory for each ready
request at each eligible destination.
2. Compute route bids using (5.5), and record desired load at each request’s highest-bidding eligible destination
whenever that bid is nonnegative, prior to capacity filtering.
3. Process overdue requests in arrival order, followed by standard requests in decreasing order of best eligible
bid; issue an offer for each request’s highest-bidding qualifying route, reserve its capacity, and hold unplaced
requests.
4. Update work and memory prices using (5.6). When a client acts on an offer, recheck eligibility and capacity
before dispatch, and release unused offers upon expiry.
Endpoint allocator, whenever active work needs KV blocks. Reclaim unpinned blocks from the lowest nonempty
priority bucket until sufficient blocks are available or none remain eligible.
6.1. Experimental Setting, Workloads, and Benchmarks
Agent execution and cluster architecture. In each experiment, a bounded-concurrency
client manages a pool of sessions, each corresponding to one execution, or rollout, of an agent task.
Within each session, the agent alternates between LLM inference calls and external tool execution,
such as running shell commands or tests in containerized environments. Each admitted inference
request initiates a turn, and all requests within a session carry the same persistent identifier.
All cluster experiments serve the same fixed Step 3.7 Flash checkpoint (StepFun, 2026), a mixture-
of-experts (MoE) model with approximately 197 billion parameters, 45 decoder layers, and hidden
dimension 4,096 (its 42 MoE layers each activate eight of 288 routed experts per token alongside
one shared expert). Each serving replica spans eight H200 GPUs using tensor parallelism (TP8).
Consequently, the 8-, 16-, and 128-GPU deployments provide one, two, and sixteen independently
routable endpoints, respectively. No model weights are updated during measurement. A central
CPU router queries the request-scheduler over gRPC for admission and endpoint selection, while
vLLM manages token-level batching and physical KV blocks locally on each replica. Additional
telemetry, instrumentation, and hyperparameter details appear in Appendix EC.3.
Workloads. We evaluate two multi-turn software-engineering benchmarks:
• SWE: A production mixture of 2,645 software-engineering tasks drawn from SWE-Factory
(1,632) (Guo et al., 2026), SWE-rebench-v2 (975) (Badertdinov et al., 2026), and Multi-SWE-
RL (38) (Zan et al., 2025; ByteDance Seed, 2025), spanning 2,641 distinct task identifiers
across multiple programming languages.

Table 2 and Figure 1 summarize the two workloads in the three-hour PARK runs used for
Table 4. Although both workloads accumulate long prompt histories (averaging 43,168 prompt
tokens per request on SWE and 36,254 on TB), their interaction patterns differ sharply. Completed
SWE sessions average 71.87 turns with relatively short responses (mean 433.46 output tokens),
creating frequent opportunities to reuse the conversation’s prefix across rapid tool calls. By contrast,
completed TB sessions average 16.52 turns with responses approximately 5.3 times as long on average
(2,290.16 output tokens), placing substantially heavier pressure on active decode concurrency and
KV-cache capacity per turn.
Benchmark policies. Table 3 summarizes the six serving policies compared in our cluster
experiments. All five baseline policies admit every arriving prompt immediately without holding
and rely on vLLM’s native least-recently-used (LRU) eviction when an endpoint needs KV blocks;
they differ only in how they select an endpoint. Let Re and We denote running and waiting requests
at endpoint e, Be its reported pending-prefill tokens, and Ue = P −min{He,P −1} the estimated
uncached prefill tokens for a prompt of length P given longest witnessed local prefix He. The
three queue- and prefill-based baselines minimize Re + We (Shortest queue), Re + 4We (Weighted
queue), and Be (Least prefill), respectively. SGLang routing ports SGLang’s cache aware zmq
endpoint-selection rule SGLang (2026) into our shared vLLM serving stack: it routes to the endpoint
with the longest cached prefix match whenever the relative match exceeds 50% and server load
imbalance remains within configured thresholds, and otherwise selects the least-loaded endpoint. In
contrast, PARK (Algorithm 2) couples shadow-price admission and routing with priority-bucket
KV eviction. Exact tie-breaking and staleness rules appear in Appendix EC.3.

Performance metrics. Our primary serving metric is output throughput (generated tokens/s),
defined as the aggregate rate at which output tokens are produced across all replicas—computed from
each replica’s cumulative generated-token counter divided by elapsed wall-clock time, as recorded
by an independent monitor (Appendix EC.3). Because output throughput tracks continuous token
generation while requests are decoding, whereas turn throughput (completed turns/min) registers
only when a turn finishes, the two rates can diverge over a run: synchronized client release rounds
or short tool-call replies produce sharp early spikes in completed turns/min with modest token/s,
whereas long generations sustain high token/s at lower turn-completion rates. We therefore report
output tokens/s alongside completed turns/min and completed sessions.

on the two-replica (16-GPU) deployment (three hours of measurement), and Figures 2 and 3 show
the corresponding time-series trajectories on SWE and TB. On both workloads, PARK achieves
the highest output throughput, delivering 6,575 tokens/s on SWE and 8,590 tokens/s on TB.

128-GPU deployment. To verify that PARK’s centralized primal–dual control and local
eviction coordinate larger clusters under real agent traffic, we scale the deployment eightfold from
two to sixteen TP8 replicas (128 GPUs) and increase the maximum number of concurrent sessions
eightfold from 512 to 4,096 (Table 5). Over a three-hour measurement window, PARK sustains
approximately 50,789 output tokens/s on SWE, substantially outperforming the baselines (Figure 4).
The cluster completes 6,473 turns/min with a 97.42% prefix cache hit rate and an average KV
occupancy of 56.15%, and during this window, 12,295 sessions finished. In a separate three-hour
evaluation on TB at the same scale, PARK achieves 67,363 output tokens/s and 1,575 turns/min,
with 13,563 completed sessions, while maintaining a 91.32% prefix cache hit rate at an average KV
occupancy of 41.04%.

6.3. Cache Retention and Routing Behavior
Single-replica cache-retention ablation. To isolate the impact of index-based eviction from
routing, we evaluate a single eight-GPU replica (E = 1) on SWE with fixed round-robin dispatch and
a maximum of 256 pending sessions (five-minute warmup followed by 30 minutes of measurement).
Both arms use identical vLLM asynchronous scheduling and chunked prefill; only the selection of
reclaimable idle KV blocks differs between native LRU and our priority-bucket retention index
(Section 5.3).
Table 6 traces the causal chain from cache survival to serving throughput:
1. Reduced prior-prefix loss: By prioritizing intermediate-length prefixes with high expected
reuse value per byte-epoch rather than evicting purely by recency, the retention index cuts
prior-prefix token loss—the token-weighted share of previously verified prefix tokens missing

3. Higher throughput and lower latency: Freeing compute capacity from redundant prefill raises
output throughput by 36.7% (from 2,326 to 3,179 tokens/s) and reduces mean time-to-first-
token (TTFT) by 35.5% (from 25.56 s to 16.49 s).
Multi-replica endpoint affinity and cache thrashing. In multi-replica clusters, routing
and retention reinforce one another: returning a session to its cache owner creates an opportunity
for prefix reuse, which generates savings only if the prefix survives the inter-turn tool delay. In
the three-hour, 16-GPU SWE runs, PARK switched replicas on 0.14% of returning requests
(222 of 161,218), compared with 50.14% for Round robin (19,310 of 38,515). Panels C and D of
Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the operational consequence across time: baselines such as Shortest queue
accumulate high KV occupancy (Panel C) while suffering near-zero prefix hit rates (Panel D)
because cross-replica switching and recency eviction continually thrash cached prefixes, whereas
PARK maintains moderate KV occupancy (≈50% on SWE) alongside a ≈98% prefix hit rate.
7. Conclusion
Multi-turn AI agents transform LLM serving from stateless request dispatch into a dynamic resource-
allocation problem with endogenous state: routing determines where a conversation’s prefix can
next be reused, whereas cache retention determines whether that prefix survives inter-turn delays.
By formulating a fluid approximation of this joint system, we characterized optimal admission,
routing, and eviction through endpoint-specific shadow prices for computation and memory coupled
with session continuation values (Theorem 4.1). Building on this decomposition, we developed a
synchronous buffer-reserve policy (Algorithm 1) and proved that setting aside a capacity reserve of
order √nlog n keeps emergency interventions rare and achieves an O(√nlog n) completion shortfall
relative to the fluid benchmark (Theorem 5.2).
To bring these structural principles to production clusters characterized by asynchronous arrivals,
delayed load reports, and engine-local memory management, we designed PARK (Algorithm 2).
PARK pairs projected subgradient price updates and one-turn migration lookahead at a central
controller with a priority-bucket KV retention index based on reuse value per byte-epoch at each
endpoint. Across 16- and 128-GPU deployments serving multi-turn software-engineering workloads
(Section 6), PARK outperforms both load-balancing and prefix-aware baselines across contrasting
interaction regimes, adapting between long-horizon, short-reply trajectories (SWE) and memory-
intensive, long-generation trajectories (TB). The single-replica ablation demonstrates the benefit
of value-aware cache retention, while the multi-replica measurements document PARK’s high
prefix-reuse rates.

EC.1.1. Single-session values and optimal resource prices

(m, em,y,z) for its flows and F(x) for its objective. All state sums below are over the finite live state
space. The transition kernels are sub-stochastic, with missing mass representing departure.

This bound is attained. Starting from m0, at every epoch send each state’s available arrival mass
to an action maximizing As,a. Propagate the resulting flows through the transition equations,
and assign each pre-retention idle population to a maximizing KEEP or DROP action. Continue
through the finite horizon. The resulting nonnegative flows satisfy every equation defining X.
Every positive routing or retention flow has zero slack, so Eτ = 0 at every epoch. Consequently,
maxx∈X L(x;λ,γ) = D(λ,γ).
Finally, take an optimal full LP dual solution with resource prices (λ⋆,γ⋆) and flow-equation
multipliers bd. Write the flow equations as Ax = b. By full dual feasibility and strong duality,
L(x;λ⋆,γ⋆) + bdT(b −Ax) ≤Vt0(m0),
x ≥0.
Indeed, the left side has nonpositive variable coefficients and constant term equal to that dual’s
objective. For x ∈X, b −Ax = 0; maximizing therefore gives D(λ⋆,γ⋆) ≤Vt0(m0). Conversely, any
optimal capacity-feasible flow x⋆has nonnegative resource slacks, so
Vt0(m0) = F(x⋆) ≤L(x⋆;λ⋆,γ⋆) ≤D(λ⋆,γ⋆).
Thus equality holds. In particular, pairing optimal prices with any optimal primal flow makes every
term in (EC.1.5) zero, as used in the bid-price theorem.
EC.1.2. Proof of the bid-price characterization
Proof of Theorem 4.1. According to (EC.1.5) in Lemma EC.1.1, complementary slackness for a
routing variable gives ys,e(t){ηs(t)−As,e(t)} = 0. A positive flow therefore uses an action maximizing
As,e(t). Since
As,e(t) −As,0(t) = Bs,e(t)
(e ∈E0),


--- Page 38 ---
e-companion
ec5
subtracting the common rejection value preserves the action ordering and proves part (a).
For an owned idle state, complementary slackness gives
zs,K(t){ws(t) −vs(t + 1) + γo(s)(t)bs} = 0,
zs,D(t){ws(t) −vE(s)(t + 1)} = 0.
Write g = ∆s(t + 1) −γo(s)(t)bs, the KEEP value minus the DROP value. If g > 0, the boundary
maximum is KEEP, and the DROP slack equals g. Hence zs,D(t) = 0, and retention conservation
implies zs,K(t) = ems(t + 1). If g < 0, the maximum is DROP, and the KEEP slack is −g. Thus
zs,K(t) = 0 and zs,D(t) = ems(t + 1). If g = 0, both slacks vanish. Tied routing actions likewise have
zero slack, leaving their allocation to the flow and capacity constraints. This proves part (b) and
the tie statement.
EC.1.3. Cache length, return time, and retention
EC.1.3.1. The value available at the next prompt
Suppose a finite return has positive
probability. A policy π starts with the cache available at that return, observes the date and prompt
information, and is nonanticipative thereafter. Let N π count its completions through H and let
Cπ contain its execution, active-memory, and subsequent idle-memory charges. Pre-return waiting
charges are excluded. Define
ε(L) = inf
π
max
1≤h≤N
P(T =h)>0
{R −Eπ[N π −Cπ | T = h]}.
(EC.1.9)
This is the smallest worst-date shortfall from R; each date’s value averages over its prompt and
subsequent service.
Let sh denote the observed cached state at a return in epoch t + h. Starting from idle, admitted
turns minus the terminal active indicator equals completed turns on every sample path. The
admission rewards and terminal values in the backward recursion therefore make ηsh(t + h) the
optimal expected completions minus resource charges. Backward induction selects a maximizing
action at every state and date, including every boundary-retention decision. The resulting policy is
optimal from every return state simultaneously. Every other policy has weakly smaller value at
each state and hence at each return date. It follows that
ε(L) =
max
1≤h≤N
P(T =h)>0

R −E[ηsh(t + h) | T = h]
	
.
(EC.1.10)
The bound R and nonnegative charges give an upper value bound of R. Rejecting every prompt
and dropping every cache gives value zero. Consequently 0 ≤ε(L) ≤R and
R −ε(L) ≤E[ηsh(t + h) | T = h] ≤R
(EC.1.11)
for every possible return date.

EC.1.3.2. Proof of the retention and eviction conditions
Proof of Proposition 4.2. Let us first briefly talk about the proof idea. We first bound the additional
value of having the cache when the next prompt arrives. We then express retention as choosing how
long to wait for that prompt, and subtract the storage charge from the expected benefit. Retention is
optimal if some waiting deadline has positive gain; eviction is optimal if every positive deadline has
negative gain. The quantity deff allows us to obtain the stated conditions from these comparisons.
Fix the current cached state s and write s0 = E(s). All probabilities below condition on the
current information, and all values use the same fixed dual prices. If N = 0 or no return is possible,
keeping the cache pays γbs > 0 without providing future value, so eviction is optimal. Henceforth a
finite return has positive probability. For brevity, put
C = λ(a1L + a2L2),
D = ¯λe(a1L + a2L2),
where C bounds the first cold turn’s expected execution charge from below, and D bounds reuse
savings from above under the additional assumption for the short-cache comparison.
Step 1: Bound the benefit at the next prompt. For each h with P(T = h) > 0, let sh be the
cached state observed when the prompt arrives in epoch t + h, and let s0

counterpart. Define
gh = E[ηsh(t + h) −ηs0
h(t + h) | T = h].
(EC.1.12)

routing and retention decisions, but excludes the storage charges paid before that return.
We first show that the cache-free value is at most [R −C]+. Consider any continuation policy µ
starting without the cache at this return. Let N µ count its completed turns through H, and let Cµ
be all its resource charges from the return through H. Define the first admission epoch by

Step 2: Calculate the value of a waiting deadline. Before the next prompt, a deterministic
policy observes only continued nonarrival and the resulting idle age. Along this no-return history, it
has a first eviction date, which defines a deadline u ∈{0,...,N}. Deadline u = 0 means immediate
eviction. A positive deadline keeps the cache available for prompt epochs t + 1,...,t + u, and evicts
it at the boundary ending t + u if no prompt has arrived. Waiting beyond the final prompt epoch
provides no terminal value.

A service-cost example. An incremental work model with m new tokens has profiles
cold:
a0 + a1(L + m) + a2(L + m)2,
warm:
a0 + a1m + a2(2Lm + m2).
Their difference is a1L + a2L2: tokenwise work contributes the linear term and attention within
the old prefix contributes the quadratic term. New tokens still attend to that prefix when it is
cached (Vaswani et al., 2017; Hugging Face, 2026).
Suppose the warm turn uses at most m new tokens, its total execution work is bounded by the
warm profile, and its active footprint is at most β(L + m). If ¯λe and ¯γe bound the execution and
active-memory prices over the remaining horizon, then
Cw
e (h,L) ≤¯λe[a0 + a1m + a2(2Lm + m2)] + ¯γeβH(L + m) = c0 + c1L,
(EC.1.23)
c0 = ¯λe(a0 + a1m + a2m2) + ¯γeβHm,
c1 = 2¯λea2m + ¯γeβH.
The completion bound q0 is evaluated separately from the service kernels. Both the warm upper
bound and cold lower bound count work actually charged by H.
The same policy-evaluation argument allows several future turns. If a specified policy has expected
completions at least Q and expected charges at most c0 + c1L at every possible return date, then
ε(L) ≤R −Q + c0 + c1L, and (EC.1.21) holds with Q replacing q0.

EC.1.3.4. Return distributions and the age comparison
For two residual return times
T1 ≤st T2 (meaning that P(T1 > u) ≤P(T2 > u) for every u) over the same remaining horizon, every
deadline satisfies
E[min(T1,u)] ≤E[min(T2,u)],
P(T1 ≤u) ≥P(T2 ≤u).
Thus each positive-denominator ratio for T2 is weakly smaller for T1, and T1 may have additional
eligible deadlines. Minimization gives deff(T1) ≤deff(T2), with the same infinity convention.
Proof of Corollary 4.3. At an age a with P(U > a | L) > 0, define
Sa(h) = P(U > a + h | U > a,L),
Sa(0) = 1.
Let Ta be the residual return time, with returns beyond the common horizon N recorded as ∞. For
h ≤N, P(Ta = h) = Sa(h −1)p(a + h −1,L). The identity min(Ta,u) = Pu
h=1 1{Ta ≥h} gives, for
1 ≤u ≤N,

u
X
h=1

P(Ta ≤u)
E[min(Ta,u)] =

The denominator is positive. If the hazard is nonincreasing, this weighted average is at most p(a,L),
with equality at u = 1. Taking reciprocals of the maximum ratio gives deff(a,L) = 1/p(a,L) when
p(a,L) > 0. If p(a,L) = 0, all subsequent hazards vanish, so both sides are infinite. The expression
is nondecreasing in age.
If the hazard is nondecreasing, then P(Ta > h) = Qh−1
r=0(1 −p(a + r,L)), h ≤N. Every factor is
weakly smaller at an older age, so its residual return time is stochastically smaller. The ordering
proved above makes deff nonincreasing in age. Constant hazard gives deff = 1/p, independently of
age.

Using the lower bound on gh at a minimizing deadline proves the retention certificate. Using either
upper bound at every deadline with F(u) > 0 proves the corresponding eviction certificate. A
deadline with F(u) = 0 has gain −bsWγ(u) ≤0. Hence eviction is optimal under either strict eviction
inequality; it is the unique initial action if γe(t) > 0, because every positive deadline then incurs a
strictly positive charge.
If warm-service bounds are available only for returns in the first m ≤N epochs, the retention
test can restrict both the deficit’s maximum and the deadline minimum to this range. Its proof
chooses a deadline u ≤m and therefore uses only these bounds. Eviction tests continue to use all
possible return dates and deadlines.
EC.2. Proofs for the buffer-reserve policy
Notation and the emergency rule. Fluid populations and flows in this appendix are divided
by n. Write
δn = rn/n = b
p
log n/n,
Wt(m;c) = NA(m) + Vt(m;c),
where c collects execution and memory capacities over the remaining horizon. The nominal profile is
ct; the profile used by the buffered LP at t is c−,n;t
t
, with entries Be−(τ −t+1)δn and Ge−(τ −t+1)δn
for τ ≥t. Thus Wt(m) in the main text means Wt(m;ct). An implemented quota is ⌊nys,e⌋or
⌊nzs,K⌋in these units.
For the analysis, the potential ordinary epoch follows the quota decisions and the ordinary service
laws without intervention. The theoretical emergency mechanism in Section 3 enforces the actual
capacity constraints causally. We use its following property: it leaves the epoch unchanged whenever
the potential ordinary execution loads and post-retention boundary-memory loads fit. Otherwise
it can stop admissions, interrupt unfinished work, and release memory before the corresponding
constraint is violated. An infeasible reoptimization also triggers the emergency rule. Previously
completed turns keep their rewards, and interrupted turns earn none. This specifies the safety
mechanism used in the theorem; future potential loads are used only in its probability analysis.
Let ¯ν = maxτ
P
s νs(τ) and Kτ = K0 + τ(¯ν + 1). The estimates below are uniform over histories
with ∥M (n)(τ)∥1 ≤Kτn. On the good successor events used below, the next population satisfies the
corresponding bound with Kτ+1. Constants may depend on K0,H, the fixed primitives, and b, but
not on n or the history.
EC.2.1. Two properties of the fluid LP
We first establish a uniform fluid-value regularity.


--- Page 46 ---
e-companion
ec13
Lemma EC.2.1. There is a finite constant L, uniform over starting epochs, such that any two
feasible parameter pairs satisfy
|Wt(m;c) −Wt(m′;c′)| ≤L
␀∥m −m′∥1 + ∥c −c′∥1

.
The same conclusion holds for Vt. Both values are nondecreasing in each capacity coordinate.
Proof. Sub-stochastic transitions and flow conservation give
∥m(τ + 1)∥1 ≤∥m(τ)∥1 +
X
s
νs(τ).
This bounds every population variable over the finite horizon. Arrival and retention conservation
then bound every action variable. Each feasible instance consequently has a finite attained optimum.
Add resource slacks, remove linearly dependent equality rows, and write the remaining LP as
max{f ⊤x : Ax = d + Dm + Fc, x ≥0},
where the matrices are fixed and A has full row rank. The dual feasible set {v : A⊤v ≥f} is nonempty
by LP strong duality. This polyhedron has no line: a line direction would satisfy A⊤v = 0, and full
row rank forces v = 0. It therefore has finitely many vertices v1,...,vJ, and a finite attained dual
optimum occurs at a vertex. For every feasible parameter pair,
Vt(m;c) = min
1≤j≤J(vj)⊤(d + Dm + Fc).
Let L0 be the largest infinity norm of the slope vectors ((vj)⊤D,(vj)⊤F) of these affine functions.
If j′ minimizes at (m′,c′), evaluation of the same affine function at (m,c) gives
Vt(m;c) −Vt(m′;c′) ≤L0(∥m −m′∥1 + ∥c −c′∥1).
Interchanging the pairs proves the absolute bound. Adding NA(m) increases the constant by at
most one. Enlarging capacities enlarges the feasible set, proving monotonicity. Taking the largest
constant over the finitely many starting epochs gives L.

flow equations. The stated capacity increase covers every added load.

EC.2.3. Current safety and feasibility of the next plan
The following lemma shows that a sufficiently large capacity reserve absorbs single-epoch stochastic
fluctuations without emergency intervention and preserves feasibility of the buffered linear program
across the horizon with high probability.
Lemma EC.2.4. For any q > 0, choose b (from (5.3)) sufficiently large. At a history with a feasible
buffered LP and ∥M (n)(t)∥1 ≤Ktn, there is an event of conditional probability at least 1 −Cn−q on
which the current epoch needs no intervention and the next buffered LP is feasible. On this event,
∥M (n)(t + 1)∥1 ≤Kt+1n. Starting from a feasible buffered LP and ∥M (n)(t)∥1 ≤K0n, the probability
of an emergency during the remaining horizon is at most Cn−q.

buffered LP remains feasible, and finally combine these bounds over the horizon. All current-epoch
coefficients suppress their argument t.

Proof of Theorem 5.2. The routing decisions use current arrivals and previously filled quotas;
retention uses the observed boundary states. The emergency mechanism is causal and enforces

Proof of Remark 5.3. Let Cπ and Dπ count completed and interrupted turns over the
remaining horizon under policy π. An interruption ends the current turn and releases its active
memory, and incurs a penalty ϖ independent of n, whose value will be specified later. Work already
performed counts against capacity. The affected session may depart or become idle.
Form the normalized expected flow vector x ≥0 as in Lemma EC.2.5, using actual states and
decisions and taking the resource slacks to be expected unused capacities divided by n. Write


--- Page 57 ---
ec24
e-companion
Ax = h for the nominal fluid equations in the standard form of Lemma EC.2.1. Then, for a constant
k depending only on the per-turn resource bounds,
∥Ax −h∥1 ≤k EDπ/n.
To see this, assign each initially active or newly admitted turn its potential uninterrupted outcome
for the current epoch, using its conditional law at epoch start or at routing, respectively. These
potential outcomes have the means used in the fluid equations. This calculation allows the subsequent
interruption decision to depend on observed usage. Each interruption changes one session’s successor
state, a discrepancy of at most two in ℓ1, and saves at most one turn’s bounded execution and
active-memory requirements for that epoch. Arrival and retention balances hold exactly for the
observed states. Summing over epochs gives the displayed bound.
Let f be the fluid objective vector and v an optimal nominal dual vertex. By Lemma EC.2.1, we
may take ∥v∥∞≤U uniformly over starting epochs and feasible instances. Since A⊤v ≥f and x ≥0,
f ⊤x ≤v⊤h + v⊤(Ax −h) ≤Vt(m;ct) + Uk EDπ/n.
Each interrupted turn must also be subtracted when converting admissions into completions. The
completion accounting identity therefore gives
E[Cπ −ϖDπ] = n[NA(m) + f ⊤x] −(1 + ϖ)EDπ ≤nWt(m) + (Uk −1 −ϖ)EDπ.
Thus any fixed ϖ ≥max{0,Uk −1} suffices for the fluid upper bound.
Finally, choose b large enough to take q = 4 in Lemma EC.2.4. Over the fixed horizon, each
session submits at most one prompt per epoch, so DBR is at most (H +1) times the total number of
initial and newly arriving sessions. The bounded normalized initial population and Assumption 5.1
give E[(DBR)2] = O(n2). Since DBR = 0 outside the emergency event En, Cauchy–Schwarz gives
EDBR ≤
␀E[(DBR)2]P(En)
1/2 = O(1/n).
The expected penalty is therefore O(1/n) for fixed ϖ. Combining this estimate with (5.4) and the
fluid upper bound proves the claim.
EC.3. Experimental Details and Hyperparameters
EC.3.1. Telemetry, Prefix-Reuse Measurement, and Baseline Implementation
Control loop and telemetry. In all cluster runs, vLLM asynchronously publishes per-replica
running and waiting request counts, pending prefill tokens, KV block utilization, and prefix-reuse
counters to the request-scheduler over gRPC at a nominal one-second cadence. Under PARK,
replicas additionally send sequenced admission and completion acknowledgments to reconcile in-
flight reservations. An independent monitoring process (Prometheus) polls each replica’s cumulative
generated-token counters every five seconds using actual request timestamps to compute fleet output
throughput.


--- Page 58 ---
e-companion
ec25
Intrinsic prefix-hit estimator. Because vLLM’s native prefix hit rate divides reused tokens
by total queried prompt tokens, new prompt text registers as a miss even when the entire prior
history remains cached. To provide feedback on retained history without external KV transfer, each
replica maintains an intrinsic-hit estimator using rotating Bloom filters over chained block hashes
(excluding preempted lookups). For an admitted lookup j, let bIj denote the reusable prefix length
(in blocks) present in the engine’s bounded local history and Aj the actual local hit length, yielding
recomputation gap Grec
j
= (bIj −Aj)+. When positive intrinsic mass is observed, the background
publisher increments cumulative feedback counters by
δQRS = b
X
j
bIj,
δHRS = b
X
j
(bIj −Grec
j ),
where b is the block-to-token scale. The window ratio ∆HRS/∆QRS measures the fraction of locally
seen historical prefixes successfully retained, falling back to ordinary hit/query counts when intrinsic
mass is zero.
Baseline tie-breaking, staleness, and cohort replenishment. All baseline routing con-
trollers and the SGLang routing port exclude replicas whose latest heartbeat is older than 5 seconds,
holding requests for a 500-ms recheck if no fresh replica is available. Equal routing scores are broken
by a rotating cursor over a fixed replica ordering (or lowest replica index in the SGLang port).
Upon dispatch, each baseline immediately increments We by one and Be by Ue (or P for Least
prefill) until the next heartbeat overwrites these estimates; TB’s Shortest queue wrapper instead
retains all dispatches from the preceding one-second window across heartbeats. For the SGLang
routing port (revision a176ba2f7b74), load is Le = Re +We, complete prompt blocks are Q = ⌊P/b⌋,
and matched blocks are he = min{Q,⌊He/b⌋}; the controller falls back to minimum load when
Lmax −Lmin > 32 and Lmax > 1.1Lmin, or when maxe he/Q ≤0.5 (evaluated in 32-bit floating point).
All runs in Table 4 continuously replenish completed sessions throughout the three-hour window,
beginning at the first vLLM request admission with no excluded warmup or concurrency ramp.
EC.3.2. PARK Implementation Details and Hyperparameters
Forecasts available before dispatch. Let P and O denote the realized prompt and output

of completed model-wide observations and DiX the subset belonging to request i’s session. Given an
initial prior mean X0 and prior weight κ, the empirical Bayes forecasts are computed via hierarchical
shrinkage:

Inherited work IeW aggregates pending prefill tokens, dispatch reservations awaiting engine acknowl-
