where ℓe = maxj Iej/Cej is the normalized load at endpoint e, θ is the current time, and θbind
i
is the
session’s most recent endpoint-binding time. The load-gap timer resets whenever the load advantage
falls below gload, a status snapshot becomes stale, or an engine restarts.
One control round. Every δ seconds, the controller reconciles status snapshots with sequenced
events, releases completed reservations, and purges expired offers. It excludes stale endpoints and
resets an endpoint’s dual prices and timers upon detecting an engine restart; if no endpoints are
fresh, all pending requests remain on hold. Each session contributes at most one ready request
and is eligible only if it has no turn or offer currently in flight. Within each round, the controller
executes three steps in sequence:
1. Measure desired load. For each ready candidate i with a nonempty eligible endpoint set Ei,
let bi = maxe∈Ei sie and let e⋆
i attain this maximum. Candidates are processed in arrival order,
breaking ties by lower current maximum normalized desired load at the endpoint and then by
fixed endpoint index. Writing cie,W = wie and cie,M = mie, desired load is
Dej = Iej + Aej +
X
i: Ei̸=∅
1{e⋆
i = e, bi ≥0}cie,j,
where the sum runs over all ready candidates. Note that the nonnegativity filter bi ≥0 applies
here even for overdue requests that will receive priority during allocation.
2. Issue offers. Overdue requests (ai ≥τFIFO) are served first in arrival order, followed by remaining
candidates in decreasing order of bi (breaking ties by earlier arrival). For each request, eligible
endpoints are evaluated in descending order of sie, breaking ties by smaller prospective peak
utilization maxj(Cej −rej + cie,j)/Cej. The controller selects the first unprotected endpoint
satisfying cie,j ≤rej for both resources (j ∈{W,M}) and sie ≥0, waiving only the bid sign test
for overdue requests. Once selected, the offer’s resource charges are immediately deducted from
rej. If an overdue request cannot be accommodated immediately, the controller protects its
top-ranked destination against subsequent offers in the same round so that existing work can
drain. Unplaced requests remain on hold.
3. Update prices and reconcile dispatches. Initialized at zero, dual prices are updated via (5.6) using
the desired loads recorded prior to allocation and carried forward to the next round. Issued offers
expire after τoffer seconds. When a client acts on an offer, the controller re-verifies offer validity,
snapshot freshness, engine identity, cache ownership, migration safeguards, absence of an in-flight
turn, and residual budgets net of other live offers. If all checks pass, the controller binds the
request to the endpoint, records a dispatch reservation, and forwards the request; otherwise, it
releases the offer and returns the request to the queue.


--- Page 61 ---

e-companion
From a session’s retention score to physical blocks. The idle age a in (5.7) measures the
elapsed time since the session’s previous turn completed; when estimating return-time distributions
from historical logs, sessions that remain idle at the end of the observation window are treated
as right-censored. Substituting the capped return gain and bs = βL into (5.7) yields the length-
normalized index
bIproxy(L,a) =
1
β c
deff(a,L)
min
( bR
L ,λe(a1 + a2L)
)
.
Given a discrete nondecreasing priority map Q with Q(0) = 0, the aggregate eviction priority of
physical KV block b at endpoint e is
πe(b) =
X
i∈Se(b)
Q(bIi),
where Se(b) denotes the set of sessions sharing block b and bIi is session i’s retention index. For
instance, if two sessions map to priorities 4 and 2, their private blocks receive priorities 4 and 2,
whereas their shared prefix blocks receive priority 6. Maintaining unpinned blocks in persistent
priority buckets allows the local allocator to reclaim the lowest-priority eligible block in O(1) bucket
operations without scanning all idle sessions upon every allocation.
A session with a zero retention index contributes zero weight. For a positive index I, the map
Q rounds 232I down to a power of two and clips the result to [1,230]. Each reclaimable block is
assigned to a bucket according to the sum of its sessions’ weights. Bucket 0 holds blocks of zero total
weight. The lower bounds for buckets 1 through 31 are 1,2,4,. . . ,230, respectively. The allocator
reclaims the block that entered the lowest nonempty bucket earliest. A block that changes buckets
joins the tail of its new bucket.
The endpoint queues a session for rescoring when a turn finishes or a return arrives. While a
session remains idle, its next refresh is due one second after its previous refresh completes. Each
scheduler step starts at most four session lookups and updates at most 256 block contributions,
subject to a soft time budget of 0.5 ms.
When a session ends, the worker closes the session at the router. At the endpoint, an idle forecast
expires 120 seconds after the last turn completes if no return is pending. If a compatible return is
already queued, its idle claim ends when the request attaches to the cached prefix. As sessions gain
or lose a claim on a block, the endpoint adds or subtracts each affected session’s contribution and
updates the bucket using the new total. For example, a block with contributions of 4 and 2 starts in
bucket 3. Withdrawing the 4-unit contribution leaves a total of 2 and moves the block to bucket 2.
The cached data remain in place until an allocation reclaims the block with zero active references.
Experimental settings. Table EC.1 lists the parameter values used for PARK (Algorithm 2)
across the cluster experiments. In particular, we set bR = 131,072 as a fixed reference-value cap,
calibrated to the linear work of rebuilding a full context at a reference execution price of one.
